title: The Navy's Missing Welders Are Stocking Shelves
gist: U.S. shipyards remain 174,000 workers short, and Navy-funded wage raises only reached people already in shipyard jobs. Gilroy argues the untapped labor pool is low-wage retail and food-service workers who cannot afford unpaid training, and proposes prior-year-earnings reporting, a roughly $11,000-per-worker 'wage bridge' funded by redirecting advertising money, and regional intermediaries.

insights.claim: U.S. Navy shipyards remain about 174,000 workers short despite recent Navy-funded wage increases.
insights.speaker: Michael Gilroy
insights.so_what: Labor scarcity is a binding constraint on naval shipbuilding output and delivery schedules for defense primes.
insights.quote: The yards are still 174,000 workers short.
insights.locator: The U.S. Navy's May 2026 shipbuilding plan

insights.claim: In April 2026 the Government Accountability Office told a House panel that none of the seven yards building U.S. Navy ships was positioned to meet delivery goals, citing workforce and yard infrastructure as the two reasons.
insights.speaker: Michael Gilroy
insights.so_what: Expect continued schedule slips across all Navy shipbuilding programs, affecting contractor revenue timing and fleet-size projections.
insights.quote: none of the seven yards building the Navy’s ships was positioned to meet its delivery goals

insights.claim: First-year attrition across U.S. Navy shipyards runs 50 to 60 percent, according to testimony by then-acting Navy acquisition executive Brett Seidle in March 2025.
insights.speaker: Michael Gilroy
insights.so_what: High churn means hiring numbers overstate net workforce growth at shipbuilders.
insights.quote: first-year attrition across the yards runs 50 to 60 percent

insights.claim: Shipyard pay premiums have collapsed: a shipyard job once paid three or four times comparable work and now pays only 1.2 to 1.4 times as much, per Brett Seidle's House testimony.
insights.speaker: Michael Gilroy
insights.so_what: Eroded wage premium explains recruiting weakness and implies sustained upward wage pressure on shipbuilder labor costs.
insights.locator: In addition, if shipyard pay fell behind

insights.claim: Huntington Ingalls Industries announced in April 2025 it would step back from hiring green shipbuilders and pay for experience instead, and later credited a Navy-funded wage increase at Newport News with more experienced hires and lower attrition.
insights.speaker: Michael Gilroy
insights.so_what: Primes are bidding up experienced tradespeople, which poaches from suppliers and other industries rather than growing the total pool.

insights.claim: Wage increases at Electric Boat and Newport News Shipbuilding got both yards to their required 2025 hiring rate and cut attrition by two to five percent, per the Navy's May 2026 shipbuilding plan.
insights.speaker: Michael Gilroy
insights.so_what: Navy-funded wage subsidies are working at the margin for primes, suggesting continued government funding of contractor labor costs.
insights.locator: The U.S. Navy's May 2026 shipbuilding plan

insights.claim: Because primes rationally chase experienced tradesmen, the entry-level labor market for shipbuilding is effectively uncontested and open to a new kind of intermediary.
insights.speaker: Michael Gilroy
insights.so_what: Signals a business opportunity for workforce intermediaries and training providers serving the defense industrial base.
insights.quote: The low end of the market is now up for grabs.

insights.claim: BLS data for May 2025 show about 3.09 million cashiers (median $33,180), 3.85 million fast-food and counter workers ($32,150) and 3.90 million retail salespersons ($37,310), versus welder median pay of $53,750.
insights.speaker: Michael Gilroy
insights.so_what: A roughly 10-million-person low-wage service pool is the realistic recruiting base for industrial reshoring and shipbuilding.

insights.claim: An entry-level welder at Newport News now starts near $57,000 after Navy-funded raises, so end-of-training pay is no longer the barrier; the barrier is months without a paycheck during training.
insights.speaker: Michael Gilroy
insights.so_what: Workforce policy that funds income during training, rather than higher wages, may be the more efficient lever for industrial labor supply.
insights.quote: the pay at the end of the training program is no longer the problem, but getting there means quitting a job and going months without a paycheck

insights.claim: Thirty-seven states fund community colleges on full-time-equivalent student counts, which discourages offering small early-morning classes that would let working adults keep their paid shifts.
insights.speaker: Michael Gilroy
insights.so_what: Headcount-based funding structurally misaligns public training supply with the needs of career-switching workers.
insights.quote: Thirty-seven states fund their two-year colleges on a count of full-time-equivalent students
insights.locator: Any community college could offer that class

insights.claim: A 34-year-old career switcher with a mortgage is likely a different and potentially more durable hire than the untrained 19-year-olds who set the yards' poor first-year attrition record.
insights.speaker: Michael Gilroy
insights.so_what: If true, recruiting older career-changers could materially cut shipyard churn costs.
insights.locator: There are potential risks in paying students

insights.claim: The Navy's submarine industrial base recruiting campaign spent about $100 million in FY2023 to produce roughly 9,700 hires, about $10,000 per retained hire once first-year quitters are counted.
insights.speaker: Michael Gilroy
insights.so_what: Advertising-heavy recruiting is costly per retained worker, suggesting budget could be redirected to more effective tools.
insights.quote: The Navy already spends a training paycheck on every recruit. It just spends it on advertising.
insights.locator: The second change is to pay the worker

insights.claim: A proposed 'wage bridge' of fifteen weeks at forty hours and $18 an hour would cost about $11,000 per worker, comparable to existing per-hire advertising spend.
insights.speaker: Michael Gilroy
insights.so_what: Shows a budget-neutral path to expanding shipyard labor supply that policymakers could adopt.
insights.locator: The second change is to pay the worker

insights.claim: The Navy should require every workforce program it funds to report participants' prior-year earnings, using existing state quarterly wage records, to distinguish poaching of existing welders from genuinely new entrants.
insights.speaker: Michael Gilroy
insights.so_what: Such a metric would reveal whether workforce dollars expand the labor pool or just reshuffle it among defense suppliers.
insights.quote: A program whose placements earned $50,000 the year before enrollment poached welders from elsewhere.

insights.claim: Workforce Pell, live since July 1, covers tuition for short training programs but not lost wages, and ties funding to 70 percent completion, 70 percent placement and earnings exceeding training cost.
insights.speaker: Michael Gilroy
insights.so_what: New federal money is flowing into short-term community college programs, creating a market for eight-week credential courses.

insights.claim: Each shipbuilding region should designate one accountable intermediary, such as the Southeastern New England Defense Industry Alliance or Greater New Orleans, Inc., to pool supplier demand, screen applicants, pay trainees from day one and carry placement risk.
insights.speaker: Michael Gilroy
entities: Southeastern New England Defense Industry Alliance
insights.so_what: Second- and third-tier suppliers too small to run academies would gain access to trained labor, easing supply chain bottlenecks.

insights.claim: MDRC's ten-year WorkAdvance results found one of four sector training programs raised earnings by 32 percent after a decade while the other three showed no effect by year ten.
insights.speaker: Michael Gilroy
insights.so_what: Workforce program returns are highly variable, so funding should be tied to measured outcomes.
insights.locator: The evidence that such a business

insights.claim: No study has yet tracked an adult who quits a roughly $34,000 job to retrain into shipbuilding, so the Navy should run that trial now.
insights.speaker: Michael Gilroy
insights.so_what: The core assumption of industrial reshoring labor plans remains untested.
insights.quote: No one has yet followed an adult who quits a $34,000 job.
insights.locator: But the evidence above is about the wrong person

insights.claim: Newport News Shipbuilding's president has said a shipbuilder who lasts the first year can double the entry wage within two years.
insights.speaker: Michael Gilroy
insights.so_what: First-year retention is the key value lever for both workers and yards.
insights.locator: The intermediary faces another big risk
